title: Boats to Save People
description: Brute force to optimized: scanning for a partner versus two pointers pairing lightest with heaviest.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Given an array people representing each person's weight, and a weight limit, find the minimum number of boats needed to carry everyone across, where each boat can carry at most 2 people at a time and their combined weight cannot exceed limit.

blocks.caption: Sort the weights, then pair the lightest and heaviest remaining people whenever they fit together

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given an array people representing each person's weight, and a weight limit, find the minimum number of boats needed to carry everyone across, where each boat can carry at most 2 people at a time and their combined weight cannot exceed limit.

blocks.title: Analogy: Pairing Passengers for a Weight Limited Ferry
blocks.text: Like a small ferry that can carry at most 2 passengers per trip within a strict combined weight limit, trying to pair up the heaviest passenger with the lightest one whenever the two can travel together, to use as few trips as possible.

blocks.caption: Pair the heaviest remaining person with the lightest, when their combined weight fits the limit

blocks.text: Edge case: every person's weight exactly equals the limit
When even the two lightest people together would exceed the limit, every single person must ride alone, needing as many boats as there are people.
5. How Should We Think?

Before scanning for arbitrary partners, notice this problem is really about the hardest person to place, the heaviest one remaining, and asking: who is their best, and only meaningful, chance at sharing a boat?

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Once the weights are sorted, the heaviest remaining person's best possible partner is always the lightest remaining person, since every other remaining person is at least as heavy and would only make the combined weight larger, never smaller.

Observation 2: This means there is no need to search for a partner at all: either the heaviest person fits with the lightest remaining person, or they fit with no one remaining, since failing with the lightest is failing with everyone.

Observation 3: A two-pointer scan captures this directly: check the current lightest and heaviest together; if they fit, both are placed on this boat and both pointers move inward; if they do not fit, the heaviest goes alone and only that pointer moves inward, since the lightest person still has a chance to pair with someone else later.

Observation 4: Either way, exactly one boat is used per step, since the heaviest remaining person is always resolved, either paired or sent alone, guaranteeing the pointers converge in at most n steps total.

Whenever a pairing decision involves "who is the hardest item to place, and is their best possible partner good enough", sort first, then use two pointers to test the extreme pairing directly, since it is always the only pairing worth checking for that hardest item.

This is a slightly different flavor of the two-pointer convergence pattern than a straightforward sum-matching or area-maximizing problem: here, the greedy decision itself, always test the extremes, is the entire algorithm, with the pointer movement encoding the outcome of that one test.
6. Brute Force Solution
For every unpaired person starting from the lightest, search through every other unpaired person to find someone heavy enough to pair with, whose combined weight still fits the limit.
Step by step algorithm

items: Sort people by weight.
For each unpaired person, scan every other unpaired person looking for the heaviest one that still fits the limit when paired together.
Mark both as paired if found, or just the one person if no pairing fits, and count a boat.

codes.python:
def num_rescue_boats(people, limit):
    people.sort()
    n = len(people)
    used = [False] * n
    boats = 0
    for i in range(n):
        if used[i]:
            continue
        used[i] = True
        boats += 1
        for j in range(n - 1, i, -1):                            # scans every other unpaired person
            if not used[j] and people[i] + people[j] <= limit:
                used[j] = True
                break
    return boats


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(num_rescue_boats([3, 2, 2, 1], 3))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Sorting happens once up front, since the entire search for a partner relies on being able to scan from the heaviest end down toward a lighter match.

The inner loop scans from the last index down toward i, specifically searching from the heaviest unpaired candidate downward, since that gives the best chance of finding someone whose combined weight still fits.
Breaking out of the inner loop the moment a valid partner is found avoids wasted work, since only one partner is ever needed per boat.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every unpaired person is correctly matched with the best available partner, or left alone if none fits, so the count of boats is correct.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), scanning for a partner for every unpaired person.
Space: O(n), for the used tracking array (plus whatever the sort needs).

Limitation: since the array is sorted, the best possible partner for the lightest remaining person is always the heaviest remaining person, so scanning through every other person to find it is unnecessary.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force's inner scan searches for a valid partner among every remaining candidate, but on a sorted array, the search itself is unnecessary: the best possible partner for the lightest remaining person is always, unconditionally, the heaviest remaining person, since pairing with anyone lighter than that would only make an already-successful pairing succeed by a wider margin, never fail where the heaviest pairing would have succeeded. This means the entire question collapses to a single comparison per step, does the current lightest person fit with the current heaviest person, rather than a search through every candidate, replacing an O(n) inner scan per person with a single O(1) check.

Sort the weights, then use two pointers: one at the lightest remaining person, one at the heaviest. If the lightest and heaviest together fit the limit, pair them and move both pointers inward. If they do not fit, the heaviest person must go alone, since they cannot fit with anyone lighter either, so only move the heavy pointer inward. Either way, count one boat per step.
9. Optimized Solution
Two pointers on the sorted weights, pairing the lightest and heaviest whenever they fit together.

blocks.caption: Optimized: sort first, then pair the lightest with the heaviest whenever they fit

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by the sort.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the sort itself.
Why This Works

On a sorted array, the current right pointer always represents the heaviest person not yet placed, and the current left pointer always represents the lightest person not yet placed. If even the lightest available person cannot bring the heaviest person's boat under the limit, then by sortedness every other remaining person, all at least as heavy as the current left pointer, would make the sum even larger, so no partner exists for the heaviest person at all, and they must ride alone. If the lightest does fit, no other pairing could possibly free up more capacity for the heaviest person, since the lightest person is by definition the smallest possible addition to the boat's weight, making it the best, not just a valid, choice.

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The heaviest pointer decrements unconditionally on every iteration, since the heaviest remaining person is always resolved, either paired or sent alone, exactly once per loop pass.

The lightest pointer only advances when a successful pairing actually happens, since an unpaired lightest person remains eligible to be tried against the next heaviest candidate in a future iteration.
boats increments exactly once per iteration, regardless of whether one or two people were placed, since each iteration always resolves exactly one boat's worth of capacity.
The loop condition allows the two pointers to be equal, correctly handling the case where exactly one person remains, letting them take one final boat alone.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The greedy rule works because the heaviest remaining person can only ever be paired with the lightest remaining person, if anyone at all, since every other remaining person is even heavier and would only make the pair heavier still.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to always advance the right pointer regardless of whether a pair was formed, since the heaviest person always leaves on the current boat one way or another.

Trying to pair the heaviest person with someone other than the lightest remaining person, which can never help since the lightest remaining person is the heaviest person's best, and effectively only meaningful, chance at fitting under the limit.
Using a strict less-than loop condition instead of allowing equality, which would incorrectly skip the final single remaining person when the pointers meet at the same index.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explain why the heaviest and lightest pairing is greedy-optimal: if the heaviest person cannot fit with the lightest remaining person, they cannot fit with anyone remaining, since everyone else is at least as heavy.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Pair items under a combined constraint, minimizing the number of groups" points toward sorting first, then two pointers testing the extreme, lightest versus heaviest, pairing directly, since it is always the only pairing worth checking for the hardest-to-place item.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would this change if a boat could carry up to 3 people instead of 2? The simple two-pointer approach no longer directly generalizes, since a 3-person grouping decision is more complex; a greedy approach still often works but requires more careful casework, or a different technique such as a two-pointer scan combined with a middle pointer.

What if boats had different individual weight limits instead of one shared limit? Sorting alone would no longer suffice, since the assignment of people to boats interacts with which specific boat's limit is being tested; this becomes closer to a bipartite matching or more general assignment problem.

How would you prove this greedy approach is optimal, not just plausible? An exchange argument: in any optimal solution, if the heaviest person is paired with someone other than the lightest remaining person, swapping that pairing to use the lightest person instead never uses more boats and never breaks any other pairing, since the lightest person fits at least as easily as whoever they replace.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Same "sort, then pair extremes" greedy structure as Container With Most Water and Two Sum II, though here the greedy choice, always test the extreme pairing, is the whole algorithm, not just an efficiency trick.
Same exchange-argument justification style as Split Array into Consecutive Subsequences' "always prefer extending" rule, just applied to a pairing decision instead of a sequence-building one.
Same "the hardest item to place determines the pairing, and its only hope is the easiest available partner" reasoning appears in many greedy bin-packing and scheduling problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(n) space.
Optimized: O(n log n) time (dominated by sorting), O(1) extra space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Sort, then two pointers greedily pairing the lightest and heaviest remaining people whenever they fit
Core Idea: The heaviest remaining person's only possible partner is the lightest remaining person, since everyone else is at least as heavy, so a single direct comparison per step replaces any search
Time: O(n log n), dominated by the sort
Space: O(1) extra beyond the sort
Most Important Observation: When the hardest item to place has exactly one meaningful candidate partner, the easiest remaining one, sorting plus two pointers replaces a search entirely
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Heaviest pairs with lightest, or rides alone; either way, one boat per step
